clinicalPearls: Posterior misdirection of eyelashes from a normally positioned lid margin, so lashes rub against the ocular surface
Causes foreign-body sensation, watering, redness and, if chronic, corneal abrasion and scarring
It differs from entropion, in which the whole lid margin turns inward
Common causes include chronic blepharitis, cicatrising conditions and, globally, trachoma
Trachomatous trichiasis is a leading infective cause of blindness worldwide and a target of elimination programmes
Management ranges from epilation and cryotherapy or electrolysis to lid surgery for cicatricial disease
reference.pathophysiology: Trichiasis arises when eyelash follicles or the lid margin are distorted so that lashes grow toward the globe despite a normally positioned lid. Chronic inflammation, scarring or cicatrisation of the lid margin, as in trachoma, chronic blepharitis or other cicatrising conjunctival diseases, redirects the lashes posteriorly. The abrasive lashes irritate the cornea and conjunctiva, and persistent rubbing can cause epithelial breakdown, corneal scarring and visual loss.
additionalDifferentials: Cicatricial conjunctival disease (for example trachoma, ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of lash direction, lid margin and cornea
Fluorescein staining to assess corneal involvement
Assessment for underlying cicatricial or infective cause
Eversion of the lid to exclude entropion and scarring
Consideration of biopsy where a cicatrising immunobullous disease is suspected
redFlags: Corneal ulceration or scarring threatening vision
Features of a progressive cicatrising conjunctival disease
Signs suggesting ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid
reference.prognosis: Isolated trichiasis is readily treated by lash removal or ablation, though recurrence is common; cicatricial disease requires treating the underlying cause and may need lid surgery to protect the cornea.
pitfalls: Confusing trichiasis with entropion, which needs different surgery
Missing an underlying cicatrising disease such as mucous membrane pemphigoid
Neglecting corneal protection in chronic cases
Relying on simple epilation alone, which is often followed by recurrence
management: Mechanical lash removal by epilation for immediate relief, recognising that recurrence follows regrowth
Definitive ablation of aberrant follicles by electrolysis, cryotherapy or laser for localised, recurrent lashes
Lid rotation surgery such as bilamellar tarsal rotation for cicatricial and trachomatous trichiasis affecting many lashes
Treat the underlying cause, whether chronic blepharitis, cicatrising conjunctival disease, or trachoma with its antibiotic (azithromycin) and the wider SAFE elimination strategy
Protect the ocular surface with lubricants and, where needed, a bandage contact lens to prevent corneal abrasion and scarring
Monitor the cornea at the slit lamp with fluorescein staining for epithelial breakdown and scarring
Refer to oculoplastics for surgical correction and follow-up given the high recurrence rate
